title: Indian man jailed 27 years in Australia for fatal stabbing, faces deportation
excerpt: Robin Robin, 30, was sentenced in the Victorian Supreme Court for murdering 22-year-old Navjeet Singh Sandhu and attempting to murder Sharwan Singh during a drunken rampage in Ormond in May 2024. He will not be eligible for parole for 20 years and is expected to be deported to India.
body:
• Robin Robin, 30, was sentenced in the Victorian Supreme Court to 27 years in prison for murdering 22-year-old Navjeet Singh Sandhu and attempting to murder 30-year-old Sharwan Singh in Ormond, Melbourne, in May 2024.
  • The court imposed a 20-year non-parole period after Justice Andrew Tinney called the knife attack "unprovoked and uncalled for" and driven by "murderous anger."
  • A jury rejected Robin's self-defence claim in April; victim-impact statements from Navjeet's father and a young witness were heard at the pre-sentence hearing.
  • Robin, who fled to New South Wales with his brother before arrest, is expected to face deportation to India once his sentence ends.

A 30-year-old Indian-origin man has been jailed for 27 years in Australia for fatally stabbing a fellow student and attempting to kill another during a drunken rampage at a Melbourne house party. Robin Robin was sentenced in the Victorian Supreme Court on Friday for the murder of 22-year-old Navjeet Singh Sandhu and the attempted murder of 30-year-old Sharwan Singh in Ormond, in Melbourne's southeast, in the early hours of May 5, 2024.

The court set a 20-year non-parole period, meaning Robin — already more than two years behind bars since his arrest — cannot seek release before 2044. A jury convicted him in April after rejecting his claim that he had acted in self-defence.

Context & Background

The violence began as a celebration. Robin had been drinking whisky with friends at his Ormond home on the evening of May 4, 2024, marking his brother Abhijeet Abhijeet's purchase of a new car, according to court reporting by the Times of India and the Australian Associated Press. Sharwan Singh, Robin's housemate, left the gathering about 6.30pm to play cards at Navjeet Singh's house — without saying goodbye, a slight that enraged Robin.

An abusive string of phone calls followed. Robin demanded Sharwan return and threatened to throw his belongings into the street. Navjeet drove Sharwan back around 12.30am so he could collect his things. As Sharwan loaded the car, Robin attacked: he stabbed his housemate in the chest, then twice more in the left shoulder while shouting abuse in Hindi. When Navjeet stepped in to help, Robin grabbed him by the collar and stabbed him repeatedly as he tried to escape. Navjeet suffered fatal injuries to his heart and lungs and died; Sharwan survived. Robin and his brother fled Victoria and were arrested in New South Wales two days later. Police at the time said the brothers, on a student visa and a bridging visa, were a flight risk.

At a pre-sentence hearing, the court heard the attack's toll on witnesses and families. Ella Cross, 20, who tried to save the dying man that night, said she now lives with PTSD and anxiety: "The person I was before that night feels very different to the person I am today."

"The joy and laughter of our home have now turned into silence and endless tears."

— Jitender Sandhu, father of Navjeet Singh Sandhu, in a statement read to the court

Impact & Analysis

Justice Andrew Tinney described the attack as "unprovoked and uncalled for," said Robin had acted with "murderous anger," and called the violence "extreme and wanton."

Central to the sentence was Robin's demeanor. The judge found he had shown no genuine remorse — a finding that weighed heavily against him. "Your lack of regret and remorse for your offending has persisted until the present time," Justice Tinney said, noting that Robin had fled the scene and left his victim dying on the road "showing no concern for him at all." Defence barrister John Desmond had argued his client did feel regret and remorse, despite running a trial built on self-defence against the surviving victim. The court disagreed.

Navjeet's father, Jitender Sandhu, watched the sentencing through a video link from India and said his son's death had destroyed the hopes and dreams of the family. Navjeet was the family's only son.

"Your lack of regret and remorse for your offending has persisted until the present time."

— Justice Andrew Tinney, Victorian Supreme Court

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora in Australia — one of the country's largest migrant communities, with tens of thousands of international students — the case carries a second verdict: deportation. Robin is expected to face removal to India once his sentence is served.

Australia's Migration Act carries a character test under which visas are cancelled for non-citizens handed prison sentences of 12 months or more. A 27-year murder sentence all but guarantees cancellation, and serious convictions routinely end with deportation after release — a stark warning for Indian students and temporary visa holders.

What's Next

Robin has 28 days to appeal the conviction and sentence to the Court of Appeal. If no appeal is filed, or if one fails, the deportation process begins as he nears the end of his sentence — a two-decade horizon. Navjeet's family, meanwhile, returns to a silence that no sentence can fill.
image_caption: Melbourne, where the Victorian Supreme Court sentenced Robin Robin to 27 years in prison for a fatal stabbing in Ormond.
nri_angle: The sentencing shows how a serious criminal conviction in Australia leads to visa cancellation and post-sentence deportation for Indian nationals, a direct warning for the large Indian student and migrant community.
